title: Dynamic Programming
summary: Solving problems by combining answers to overlapping subproblems - why naive recursion explodes, memoisation (top-down), tabulation (bottom-up), the recipe of state, transition, base cases and order, counting paths in a grid, minimum coins for any coin system, counting the ways to make change, rebuilding the chosen solution, and saving memory by keeping only the rows you need.

cards.q: What two properties make a problem suitable for dynamic programming?
cards.a:
optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems

Recursion alone is not enough: DP pays off when the same subproblems repeat.

cards.q: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?
cards.a:
Recursion plus a cache, versus a loop over a table

Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches results; tabulation fills a table iteratively in an order that respects the dependencies. Both solve each subproblem once.

cards.q: In the "ways to make change" loop, why are the coins in the outer loop?
cards.a:
So each combination is counted only once

With the amounts outside, 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 would be counted as different ways; coins outside fix one order.
